title: Current advances in chemical ecology-based management tactics for the spotted lanternfly, Lycorma delicatula (Hemiptera: Fulgoridae)
content:
Abstract
The spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula [White]), an invasive fulgorid planthopper of significant economic concern, relies on a complex suite of chemical signals to navigate host selection, aggregation, and reproductive success in its US invaded range. While initial research focused primarily on volatile attraction, recent advances have broadened to include a multitrophic understanding of the insect’s chemical ecology. This review synthesizes the rapidly expanding body of literature on L. delicatula chemical ecology, with a focus on findings published since 2023, to delineate the mechanisms governing host selection, conspecific recruitment, and complex tritrophic interactions. Current management relies heavily on broad-spectrum insecticides, but studies are constantly attempting to shift the field toward more selective strategies as understanding grows regarding L. delicatula sensory biology, conspecific signaling, and host-mediated interactions. We propose that the next phase of management should move beyond viewing chemical ecology as a supplement to insecticides and instead treat semiochemical-based tactics as the foundation for integrated pest management (IPM). Specifically, we suggest the development of multimodal devices that combine host and conspecific volatiles with vibrational and visual cues tailored to specific life stages and seasonal behaviors. Future efforts should prioritize translating these ecological findings into spatially precise management tools, such as push-pull systems and attract-and-kill stations, while leveraging new genomic resources to improve semiochemical lure selectivity and efficacy. Ultimately, integrating chemical ecology into management programs should improve early detection and provide sustainable population suppression while minimizing non-target impacts.
